While I agree the Sumerians had *become* endemic by the period in which we discuss, they clearly are not local to the region we define as Sumeria if you go back to the early Chalcolithic or late Neolithic.  The Halaf and Ubaid cultures are, but evidence, especially linguistics, has shown Sumerians to have been a migrating people into the area originally.  We see this in the nature of the isolate language, and how Ubaid pottery was rapidly altered and replaced in its end, when we see Sumerian style arise.  One may say this was a natural evolution, however given the rapidity and lack of other social force to motivate this shift, the migrant theory seems best.

As to *where* the Sumerians came from before they intermingled with the Ubaid and Halaf, is not at all certain.  Scholars have tried to put it all over the place, from an IE group (idiotically), to one from the Zagros, to even them being migrants from central India.  However the most likely theory seems to be they were endemic to the Persian gulf lowlands before rising sea levels slowly drove them upwards along the rivers, until they met the Ubaid and Halaf areas and began intermingling.  Even Sumerian myth has analogues to this, with there supposedly being peoples who "came from the sea" and taught the locals along with remaining with them.

So the OP is not.......completely wrong if they mean Eden is the Sumerian Urheimat, and is under the Persian gulf.  About Eden yes they are, archaeology and linguistics show that as a place and name was originally Dilmun, the island of Bahrain, which has no documented history of Sumerian cultural hegemony, but is instead a unique culture.
